prompt: An oscillator stores phase as a fraction of a cycle. You double its requested frequency without changing the sample rate. What must happen to its phase advance per sample?

options.text: It halves, so each cycle lasts longer
options.explanation: That would lower the repetition rate rather than double it.

options.text: It doubles, while the existing phase is retained
options.explanation: Correct. Each sample must cover twice as much of a cycle; a frequency change need not restart the waveform.

options.text: It stays unchanged and only the output gain doubles
options.explanation: Gain changes level, not how quickly phase completes cycles.

options.text: It resets to zero at every block
options.explanation: Block resets discard oscillator state and generally impose the block repetition spectrum.

workedExample: The sample clock gives the same number of opportunities to advance. Completing twice as many cycles in that time requires twice the advance per opportunity. Keep the current phase so the new frequency continues from the existing position.

link.title: Digital sinusoid generators — Julius O. Smith

prompt: Using `pulse(p, width)` from the lesson (`1.0 if p < width else -1.0`), what fraction of each cycle is the output +1 when `width = 0.25`, and what width gives a square wave?

options.text: 25% high; width 0.5 gives a square wave
options.explanation: Correct. The output is +1 while phase is below the width, i.e. a quarter of the cycle. At 0.5 high and low are equal: a square wave.

options.text: 75% high; width 0.5 gives a square wave
options.explanation: The comparison is `p < width`, so it is high for the *first* 25% only.

options.text: 25% high; width 1.0 gives a square wave
options.explanation: At width 1.0 the output is +1 the whole time: a constant DC value with no sustained tone; transitions can still click and DC can use headroom.

options.text: 50% high regardless; width only changes the volume
options.explanation: Width changes the duty cycle (and hence the timbre), not just the level.

workedExample:
Phase sweeps 0 → 1 once per cycle.

```
p:     0 .. 0.25 .. 1
out:   +1   |  -1
```

High during the first quarter-cycle: 25% of the cycle. Square = equal high and low = width 0.5. Widths of zero or one give constant DC rather than a sustained oscillation; changing to or from that constant may still create a transient.

link.title: Digital sinusoid generators — Julius O. Smith
